title: Practical Frontend Refactoring: Safety Nets, Invariants & Layered Test Matrix Standardization
summary: Insights and practical engineering methodologies for large-scale codebase refactoring without regressions using a layered test matrix (TU/TI) and strict contract validation.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.introduction:
Throughout a software engineer's career, dealing with rapidly expanding codebases, escalating complexity, and technical debt is inevitable. The necessity for codebase refactoring to standardize architectures, eliminate duplication (DRY), and optimize performance is continuous.

However, the greatest fear when touching legacy code is: 'Will this change accidentally break a feature on a different screen?'. The concept of an automated 'Safety Net' and a disciplined, layered Test Matrix is what separates a seasoned senior engineer from someone who refactors on luck.
sections.multi-dimensional-evaluation:
To understand the true value of systematic refactoring, let us compare two contrasting engineering approaches:

  • 'Cowboy Refactoring' (Intuition-Driven Modification): The developer renames files and extracts components directly without comprehensive automated test coverage. Verification relies entirely on manual visual testing in the browser. Consequences: High probability of missing edge-cases on mobile viewports, unnoticed type regressions, and silent production breaks.
  • 'Test-Driven Refactoring' (Safety Net-Driven Architecture): Before a single line of code or file path is moved, behavioral contracts and core invariants are strictly locked by a multi-layered Unit and Integration Test suite. Any deviation or broken contract is immediately caught by the test runner within milliseconds.
sections.case-study-experience:
During our comprehensive portfolio and blog architecture refactoring, I implemented an automated pipeline following strict verification phases:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Dev as Software Engineer
    participant Core as Legacy Codebase
    participant Tests as Standardized Test Suite - TU and TI
    participant Clean as Refactored Clean Layer

    Dev->>Tests: 1. Setup Baseline Tests - Lock Invariants
    Tests-->>Dev: 100% Green Matrix Baseline
    Dev->>Core: 2. Atomic Extraction and Layer Relocation
    Dev->>Clean: 3. Populate Common, UI, Composite, Services
    Dev->>Tests: 4. Run Automated Verification - tsc and Vitest
    alt Type or Logic Regression Found
        Tests-->>Dev: Red Alert with exact broken contract and line
        Dev->>Clean: Refine Invariant Fixes
    else All Matrix Tests Pass
        Tests-->>Dev: 30/30 Files, 141/141 Tests Passed - 100%
        Dev->>Clean: 5. Successful Production Bundle Build
    end

Key Practical Lessons:

  • Standardized Test Identifiers (Test IDs): Clearly categorize test suites using TU-<GROUP>-XX for Unit Tests (e.g. TU-COMMON-01 for Button, TU-SERVICES-01 for BlogService) and TI-XX for Integration Tests. This enables seamless cross-referencing between architectural documentation and test output.
  • 1-to-1 Symmetric Test Directory Hierarchy: Organizing test folders as tests/unit/common/, tests/unit/ui/, tests/unit/composite/, tests/unit/services/ makes locating tests instantaneous during massive code relocations.
sections.actionable-recommendations:
To execute safe, fearless refactorings, adhere to these 4 foundational rules:

  • 1. Enforce Strict Typechecking: Run npx tsc --noEmit continuously alongside your test runner. Stripping redundant path aliases and using clean relative imports ensures the compiler flags broken paths the moment a file is saved.
  • 2. Atomic Refactoring Principle: Apply only one class of change per commit (e.g. rename a component, or relocate a service). Never alter business logic and file architecture concurrently in a single step.
  • 3. Eliminate Inline Layout Specificity in Base Components: Avoid hardcoding layout properties (like style={{ display: 'flex' }}) into reusable base components, as inline styles override CSS Grid child alignments.
  • 4. Containerized Test Parity: Run your test and build suites inside Docker containers to guarantee absolute environment parity between local development and CI/CD pipelines.
sections.open-questions-discussion:
Refactoring is fundamentally a balancing act between shipping speed and long-term code maintainability. Some thought-provoking questions for engineering teams:

  • How do you decide when to perform Incremental Refactoring versus executing a complete Greenfield Rewrite?
  • How do you articulate the business value of architecture refactoring to non-technical stakeholders when no visible user feature is added?
  • What strategies work best to maintain a strict 100% test pass rate in fast-paced product delivery teams?

title: Core Algorithms Series #01: Algorithmic Efficiency Metrics — Time & Space Complexity Analysis and Asymptotic Notations (Big-O, Big-Ω, Big-Θ)
summary: Establishing a standardized evaluation framework for algorithmic efficiency: Distinguishing Wall-clock time from the RAM Computation Model, decoupling Time vs Space Complexity (Auxiliary vs Total), and mastering asymptotic notations as the foundation for the entire series.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement:
In software engineering and systems performance tuning, the critical question every engineer must answer before deploying code to Production is: 'How fast does this algorithm run, and how much memory does it consume when user data scales by 1,000x?'.

A classic beginner pitfall is measuring execution speed with physical wall-clock timers via console.time() or System.nanoTime(). This empirical approach is inherently flawed because wall-clock duration fluctuates wildly based on CPU clock speed, hardware architecture, operating system thread scheduling, and runtime garbage collection. Computer science requires an abstract mathematical framework that measures efficiency independently of physical hardware environments.
sections.initial-approach:
The naive empirical benchmarking approach:

  • Run the algorithm on a development machine with a small sample input ($N = 100$) and record the duration in milliseconds.
  • Why this fails catastrophically: An $O(N^2)$ algorithm might execute in just 0.2ms on $N = 100$, giving developers a false sense of speed. But when $N$ scales to $10^6$ on Production, execution time balloons to over 11 days, causing complete server starvation.

We need rigorous Asymptotic Analysis to quantify how computational requirements scale as input size $N$ approaches infinity.
sections.optimization-thinking:
To rigorously benchmark algorithms across the upcoming series, I establish an evaluation model rooted in the Random Access Machine (RAM) Model of Computation across three pillar dimensions:

  1. 1. Asymptotic Notation Hierarchy:
    • Big-O ($O$): Mathematical Upper Bound — Represents the worst-case scenario. This is the primary metric for contractual SLA guarantees.
    • Big-Omega ($\Omega$): Mathematical Lower Bound — Represents the best-case theoretical execution limit.
    • Big-Theta ($\Theta$): Tight Bound — When upper and lower asymptotic bounds coincide, capturing true average behavior.
  2. 2. Decoupling Time vs Space Complexity:
    • Time Complexity: Total count of primitive operations (assignments, comparisons, arithmetic) as a function of input size $N$.
    • Space Complexity (Total Space vs Auxiliary Space): Total memory required during execution. Auxiliary Space specifically denotes the extra temporary memory allocated by the algorithm itself (excluding input storage), encompassing dynamic Heap buffers and recursive Call Stack frames.
sections.code-implementation:
Big-O growth hierarchy diagram and system memory footprints:

flowchart TD
    subgraph BigOComplexity [Big-O Growth Hierarchy]
        O1["O(1) - Constant Time"]
        OLogN["O(log n) - Logarithmic - Binary Search"]
        ON["O(n) - Linear - Single Pass"]
        ONLogN["O(n log n) - Linearithmic - QuickSort, MergeSort"]
        ON2["O(n2) - Quadratic - Nested Loops"]
        O2N["O(2^n) - Exponential Recursion"]
        ONFact["O(n!) - Factorial Permutations"]
    end

    subgraph SpaceDimensions [Memory Allocation Dimensions]
        StackMem["Call Stack Memory - Recursive Stack Frames"]
        HeapMem["Heap Dynamic Memory - Auxiliary Buffers"]
    end

    O1 --> OLogN --> ON --> ONLogN --> ON2 --> O2N --> ONFact
    ONLogN -.-> StackMem
    ONLogN -.-> HeapMem

Standard TypeScript Reference Implementations for Big-O Tiers:

  • $O(1)$ Constant Time: Array index access arr[0] or HashMap key lookup.
  • $O(\log N)$ Logarithmic Time: Binary Search halving the problem space at each iteration.
  • $O(N)$ Linear Time: Iterating through $N$ elements in a single sequential pass.
  • $O(N \log N)$ Linearithmic Time: Optimal divide-and-conquer sorting algorithms like QuickSort and MergeSort.
  • $O(N^2)$ Quadratic Time: Two nested loops evaluating all element pairs $(i, j)$.
sections.complexity-applications:
The Standardized 5-Point Evaluation Framework for the Entire Series:

Every subsequent article in this series will dissect and score algorithms using this unified standard:

  • 1. Worst-Case Time Complexity ($O$): Guarantees system resilience against adversarial inputs.
  • 2. Best/Average-Case Time ($\Omega / \Theta$): Real-world operational throughput on random distributions.
  • 3. Auxiliary Space Complexity: Transient RAM overhead across Call Stack and Heap buffers.
  • 4. Stability & In-Place Capability: Preserving relative order of identical elements with zero auxiliary array allocations.
  • 5. Scalability Threshold: Maximum safe input size $N$ to execute under 100ms in low-latency production environments.

title: Core Algorithms Series #02: Binary Search & Divide and Conquer Thinking — Optimizing Lookup from O(n) to O(log n)
summary: Deep dive into Binary Search: The 50% search space elimination principle, mitigating integer overflow in midpoint calculation, iterative vs recursive trade-offs, and practical applications in Database B-Tree indexing.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement:
Data retrieval is the most frequent primitive operation in software systems. Problem statement: Given a sorted array of $N$ integers in ascending order, locate the index of a specified target value, or return -1 if not present.

With massive datasets containing tens of millions of records ($N = 10^7$), a sub-optimal search algorithm will choke throughput and introduce unacceptable latency. The engineering objective is transitioning from naive sequential scanning to a Divide-and-Conquer paradigm with $O(\log N)$ asymptotic efficiency.
sections.initial-approach:
The naive approach (Linear Search):

  • Iterate sequentially from index zero for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) and compare each item against target.
  • Performance Evaluation:
    • Best-case: $\Omega(1)$ when the target resides at index 0.
    • Worst-case: $O(N)$ when the target is at the tail or absent. On $N = 1,000,000$, Linear Search requires up to 1,000,000 comparisons.

Core flaw: Entirely discards the structural guarantee that the collection is already sorted.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Applying the Divide-and-Conquer principle:

  1. 50% Search Space Elimination: Compare the midpoint element arr[mid] with target:
    • If arr[mid] === target: Immediate match found.
    • If arr[mid] < target: Because the array is sorted, every element to the left of mid is strictly smaller than target $ o$ Discard 50% of the array and focus on [mid + 1, right].
    • If arr[mid] > target: Every element to the right is strictly larger $ o$ Constrain the search window to [left, mid - 1].
  2. Integer Overflow Mitigation: The standard formula mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2) can overflow 32-bit signed integers when left + right > 2^31 - 1. Robust engineering pattern: Always compute mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2).
sections.code-implementation:
Search window halving progression across iterations:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Step1 [Iteration 1 - n = 8 elements]
        A1["Left: 0, Right: 7, Mid: 3 - Discard 4 elements"]
    end
    subgraph Step2 [Iteration 2 - n = 4 elements]
        A2["Left: 4, Right: 7, Mid: 5 - Discard 2 elements"]
    end
    subgraph Step3 [Iteration 3 - n = 2 elements]
        A3["Left: 6, Right: 7, Mid: 6 - Target Located"]
    end

    Step1 --> Step2 --> Step3

Production TypeScript Implementation (Iterative Pattern):

  • Iterative Pattern (Recommended): Manages two pointers left = 0 and right = arr.length - 1. Consumes zero stack frames, achieving strict $O(1)$ Auxiliary Space.
  • Recursive Pattern: Recursively invokes binarySearch(arr, left, right, target). Each invocation pushes a stack frame, consuming $O(\log N)$ Auxiliary Stack Space.
sections.complexity-applications:
Metrics Scorecard (Applying Framework from Article #01):

  • Time Complexity:
    • Best-case: $\Omega(1)$ (target matches the initial midpoint).
    • Worst/Average-case: $O(\log_2 N)$ and $\Theta(\log_2 N)$. For $N = 1,000,000$ elements, Binary Search needs at most 20 comparisons (compared to 1,000,000 in Linear Search — a 50,000x speedup).
  • Auxiliary Space: $O(1)$ Iterative, $O(\log N)$ Recursive.
  • Real-World Applications: Database Index lookup (B-Tree and LSM-Tree search), git bisect for automated regression tracking in Git histories, and Binary Search on Answer paradigms in algorithmic optimization.

title: Core Algorithms Series #03: QuickSort Deep Dive — Partitioning Mechanics, Stack Depth Trade-offs & Mitigating Worst-Case O(n²)
summary: In-depth analysis of QuickSort: Comparing Lomuto vs Hoare partitioning schemes, intelligent pivot selection via Median-of-Three, tail recursion optimization to constrain stack depth, and comparative analysis against MergeSort.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement:
Sorting is the foundational pillar of computer science, governing search performance, deduplication, and aggregation pipelines. Problem statement: Given an unsorted array of $N$ elements, rearrange them in non-decreasing order.

The engineering challenge: How can we achieve maximal raw execution speed by maximizing CPU Cache Locality while eliminating the $O(N)$ extra memory allocation required by MergeSort? QuickSort represents one of the most elegant algorithmic solutions ever conceived.
sections.initial-approach:
Naive sorting approaches (Bubble Sort / Insertion Sort):

  • Repeatedly compare and swap adjacent elements.
  • Performance Evaluation:
    • Time Complexity: $O(N^2)$ — On $N = 100,000$, comparison count hits $10^{10}$, taking minutes to complete.
    • MergeSort alternative: Reaches $O(N \log N)$ but allocates an auxiliary $O(N)$ buffer on the Heap, placing high pressure on garbage collectors.
sections.optimization-thinking:
QuickSort leverages the Partitioning Paradigm:

  1. Core Concept: Select a Pivot element. Partition the array such that all elements smaller than the Pivot are shifted to the left, and all elements larger than or equal to the Pivot are shifted to the right. Recursively sort the sub-arrays.
  2. Partitioning Schemes (Lomuto vs Hoare):
    • Lomuto Partition: Single pointer scanning left-to-right. Intuitive to write, but requires up to 3x more swap operations.
    • Hoare Partition: Two pointers moving inward from both ends. Minimizes swaps significantly and demonstrates superior real-world performance.
  3. Mitigating the $O(N^2)$ Worst-Case: Choosing the first or last element on an already-sorted array degenerates the recursion tree into an $O(N^2)$ linked list. Solution: Employ Median-of-Three (median of first, middle, last elements) or Randomized Pivot.
sections.code-implementation:
Recursive partition tree and element segregation around pivots:

graph TD
    Root["Original Array: 8, 3, 1, 7, 0, 10, 2 - Pivot: 7"]
    Left1["Left Partition smaller than 7: 3, 1, 0, 2"]
    Pivot1["Pivot: 7"]
    Right1["Right Partition larger or equal to 7: 8, 10"]
    Left2["Sub-left: 0, 1"]
    Pivot2["Pivot: 2"]
    Right2["Sub-right: 3"]

    Root --> Left1
    Root --> Pivot1
    Root --> Right1
    Left1 --> Left2
    Left1 --> Pivot2
    Left1 --> Right2

Production TypeScript Implementation with Hoare Partitioning & Median-of-Three:

  • Performs in-place element swapping directly on the original array with zero Heap allocations.
  • Tail Recursion Optimization: Always recurses into the shorter partition first, strictly bounding maximum Call Stack depth to $O(\log N)$.
sections.complexity-applications:
Metrics Scorecard (Applying Framework from Article #01):

  • Time Complexity:
    • Best/Average-case: $\Omega(N \log N)$ and $\Theta(N \log N)$. Excellent hardware cache locality due to sequential in-place memory access.
    • Worst-case: $O(N^2)$ (with Median-of-Three Pivot, probability in production is virtually zero).
  • Auxiliary Space: $O(\log N)$ (strictly for recursive stack frames, $0$ byte Heap allocation).
  • Characteristics: In-place and Non-stable.
  • Real-World Applications: Powers Array.prototype.sort() in V8 JavaScript engine, sort.Slice in Golang, and Dual-Pivot QuickSort in standard Java runtime libraries.

title: Core Algorithms Series #04: Graph Traversal Fundamentals (BFS & DFS) — Breadth vs Depth Exploration, Queue vs Stack Mechanics
summary: Mastering the two foundational graph & tree traversal paradigms: Level-by-level wavefront exploration with BFS (FIFO Queue) vs deep branch exploration with DFS (LIFO Stack/Recursion), cycle detection, and shortest path algorithms.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement:
Graph structures $G = (V, E)$ (vertices $V$ and edges $E$) model real-world networks: social relationships, GPS road networks, and package dependency DAGs.

Core problem: How do we systematically visit all vertices in a graph, determine the shortest path between two points, or detect cycles without getting trapped in infinite loops when cyclic references exist?
sections.initial-approach:
Naive unvisited exploration:

  • Traversing neighbor edges blindly. When encountering a cycle ($A o B o C o A$), the algorithm loops infinitely until memory exhaustion (Out of Memory).
  • Unbounded recursive calls trigger Call Stack Overflow errors.

Requirements: A robust Visited State Management mechanism paired with structured dispatch collections.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Decoupling the two foundational graph exploration philosophies:

  1. 1. Breadth-First Search (BFS - Level-by-Level):
    • Mechanism: Explores outward in concentric wavefronts. Visits all immediate neighbors before advancing to the next depth tier.
    • Data Structure: FIFO Queue.
    • Core Property: Mathematically guarantees finding the Shortest Path on unweighted graphs.
  2. 2. Depth-First Search (DFS - Deep Branching):
    • Mechanism: Plunges as deep as possible along each branch until a dead end is reached, then backtracks to explore remaining alternatives.
    • Data Structure: LIFO Stack or recursive Call Stack.
    • Key Strengths: Cycle Detection, Topological Sorting, and Connected Components discovery.
sections.code-implementation:
Standard vertex dispatch lifecycle sequence:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Engine as Traversal Engine
    participant Graph as Graph G(V, E)
    participant DataStruct as FIFO Queue (BFS) / LIFO Stack (DFS)
    participant Visited as Visited Set (State Tracker)

    Engine->>DataStruct: 1. Push Root vertex into structure
    Engine->>Visited: 2. Mark Root as visited
    loop While dispatch structure is non-empty
        DataStruct-->>Engine: 3. Pop current vertex U
        Engine->>Graph: 4. Query adjacency list of U
        Graph-->>Engine: Returns neighbors [V1, V2, V3]
        opt If neighbor is unvisited
            Engine->>Visited: Mark neighbor as visited
            Engine->>DataStruct: Push neighbor to Queue / Stack
        end
    end

Production TypeScript Implementation with Adjacency List:

  • Utilizes Map<string, string[]> for the adjacency graph and Set<string> for visited state tracking.
  • Function bfsShortestPath(graph, start, target) reconstructs optimal path chains efficiently.
sections.complexity-applications:
Metrics Scorecard (Applying Framework from Article #01):

  • Time Complexity: $O(V + E)$ (where $V$ is vertex count, $E$ is edge count). Every vertex and edge is processed a constant number of times.
  • Auxiliary Space Complexity:
    • BFS: $O(V)$ — In the worst case, the Queue holds all vertices at the graph's Maximum Width tier.
    • DFS: $O(V)$ — Call stack consumption is proportional to the graph's Maximum Depth.
  • Real-World Applications: Web Crawlers (BFS), social network connection degrees (Six Degrees of Separation), dependency resolution in npm and cargo (Topological Sort with DFS), and Mark-and-Sweep Garbage Collection in runtime VMs.

title: Core Algorithms Series #05: Two Pointers & Sliding Window Patterns — Transforming O(n²) Nested Loops to Linear O(n) Efficiency
summary: The craft of optimizing contiguous array and string problems: Exploiting monotonicity to transform nested O(n²) loops into linear O(n) passes, symmetric Two Pointers, and dynamic expanding/shrinking Sliding Windows.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement:
In technical interviews and real-world stream processing, contiguous subarray and substring problems account for over 40% of algorithmic tasks. Examples: Finding pairs with sum $K$, finding the longest substring without repeating characters, or finding minimal subarrays exceeding threshold $S$.

The engineering challenge: Traditional nested loops get trapped in $O(N^2)$ quadratic complexity, grinding to a halt when $N > 10^5$. Two Pointers and Sliding Window patterns represent the ultimate craft of collapsing quadratic work into strict linear $O(N)$ execution.
sections.initial-approach:
Naive Brute-Force Nested Loops:

  • Use two nested loops for i and for j to evaluate all possible index pairs.
  • Performance Evaluation: Requires $ rac{N(N-1)}{2}$ evaluations $ o O(N^2)$ time complexity. On $N = 100,000$, the CPU must compute 5 billion iterations, exceeding the 1-second timeout of web servers.

Root inefficiency: Repeatedly recalculating overlapping subproblems without taking advantage of the monotonicity of pointer movements.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Mastering two linear optimization patterns:

  1. 1. Symmetric Two Pointers (From Opposite Ends):
    • Applied on sorted arrays: Initialize left = 0 and right = n - 1.
    • Calculate sum = arr[left] + arr[right]: If sum < target $ o$ Increment left++; if sum > target $ o$ Decrement right--. Each pointer adjustment permanently eliminates candidate space without re-scanning.
  2. 2. Dynamic Sliding Window:
    • Maintain an active window $[L, R]$. Expand the right boundary R++ to incorporate incoming elements.
    • When an invariant is violated (e.g. duplicate character detected), contract the left boundary L++ until validity is restored.
    • Because both $L$ and $R$ traverse monotonically left-to-right at most $N$ times, total operations are strictly bounded to $2N o O(N)$.
sections.code-implementation:
Three-phase expand, validate, and contract sliding window lifecycle:

flowchart TD
    subgraph Phase1 [Phase 1 - Expand Right Boundary]
        Step1["Right advances rightward: Ingests new item into window"]
    end
    subgraph Phase2 [Phase 2 - Invariant Validation]
        Step2{"Is Window invariant violated?"}
    end
    subgraph Phase3 [Phase 3 - Contract Left Boundary]
        Step3["Left advances rightward: Evicts violating element"]
    end

    Step1 --> Step2
    Step2 -- Yes --> Step3
    Step3 --> Step2
    Step2 -- No --> Step1

Production TypeScript Implementation for Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters:

  • Uses a Map<string, number> to track the last seen index of each character.
  • Upon collision, jumps left = Math.max(left, lastSeenIndex + 1) directly for maximum throughput.
sections.complexity-applications:
Metrics Scorecard (Applying Framework from Article #01):

  • Time Complexity: $\Theta(N)$ — Both pointers traverse the collection exactly once. Reduces execution time from tens of seconds to under 2 milliseconds.
  • Auxiliary Space Complexity: $O(1)$ for pure Two Pointers, $O(K)$ for Sliding Window (where $K$ is the character charset size, $K \le 128$ for ASCII).
  • Real-World Applications: Streaming Analytics (sliding moving averages), API Rate Limiting (Sliding Window Log & Counter algorithms in API Gateways), and network packet compression protocols.

title: Mastering CSS Sticky in CSS Grid: Resolving Filter Drift & Parent Height Containment in Deep-Scroll Lists
summary: Deep dive into CSS Sticky containing block mechanics, resolving toolbar drift when scrolling across deep article grids, and achieving flawless 60fps rendering in React.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement:
When building rich catalog or engineering blog interfaces with a 2-column layout (Left Sidebar + Right Content Area), the search and filter controls bar is typically designed to stick at the top of the viewport (position: sticky; top: 16px;) so users can filter by category or tag at any moment.

However, during testing with 20+ articles (scroll depth exceeding 3,000px), an elusive issue emerged: when scrolling past the 15th article, the sticky filter bar drifted upward off-screen instead of staying pinned at the top. This article analyzes the root cause of CSS Sticky containing block containment and provides the definitive layout architecture to fix it.
sections.initial-approach:
The common initial implementation in React web applications:

  • Place .blog-controls-panel as a sibling alongside .blog-grid inside a shared flex parent .blog-main-inner-content (display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 20px;).
  • Apply position: sticky; top: 16px; to .blog-controls-panel.

Why did this fail? Under the CSS Positioning specification, a position: sticky element is bound to the height of its immediate containing block (its parent). As the user scrolls deep into the list, when the scroll offset reaches the bottom boundary of the parent container, the sticky element is pulled away along with the natural document flow.
sections.optimization-thinking:
To resolve this cleanly without brittle workarounds, I evaluated two strategies:

  • Strategy 1 (JavaScript Scroll Listener + position: fixed): Listen to scroll events and toggle fixed positioning. Trade-offs: Causes layout shifts, requires manual width calculations, and triggers layout thrashing / reflows on high refresh-rate monitors.
  • Strategy 2 (Encapsulate Filter Bar inside CSS Grid Container): Move .blog-controls-panel into .blog-grid as its first direct child. Because .blog-grid contains all 20+ article cards, its height naturally covers the entire scroll length of the page.

In CSS Grid, children occupy a single grid cell by default. To make the sticky filter bar span across all columns as a full-width header, I apply: grid-column: 1 / -1;.
sections.code-implementation:
Standard implementation in JSX and SCSS:

  • JSX Structure in BlogPage.tsx: Place .blog-controls-panel directly inside .blog-grid as its very first child.
  • CSS Grid & Sticky Rules: Assign grid-column: 1 / -1; position: sticky; top: 16px; z-index: 25; to .blog-controls-panel so it spans across all grid columns and sticks to the top throughout the entire scroll.
  • Smooth Glassmorphic State: Leverage backdrop-filter: blur(16px) and dynamically toggle the .is-stuck shadow class when scrolling past 40px threshold.
sections.complexity-applications:
Complexity & Performance Analysis:

  • DOM Complexity: O(1) - No extra wrapper divs or JavaScript geometry calculations needed.
  • Rendering Performance: Pure CSS sticky operates directly on the browser's GPU Compositing Layer, sustaining solid 60 FPS even on mobile devices.
  • User Experience (UX): Filter and search controls remain immediately accessible at any scroll depth, while backdrop blur ensures high legibility as cards glide underneath.

Real-World Applications: Combining position: sticky with grid-column: 1 / -1 is an ideal pattern for E-Commerce product catalogs, analytics data tables with pinned headers, and modern high-density dashboards.

title: Mastering Mermaid.js: Comprehensive Guide from Syntax to Architecture & Technical Documentation (Diagrams as Code)
summary: Practical guide to the Diagrams as Code (DaC) paradigm using Mermaid.js: Unlocking Flowchart, Sequence, Git Graph, Class, State syntax and automating architecture documentation in CI/CD pipelines.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.article-objectives:
In modern software engineering, technical documentation and architecture diagrams play a vital role in maintaining team alignment. However, traditional diagramming tools (such as Draw.io, Visio, or Lucidchart) that export static binary image files (.png, .jpg) introduce severe workflow bottlenecks:

  • Documentation Drift: When code evolves, opening graphic software, editing shapes, exporting files, and committing images is frequently skipped due to high manual friction, leaving docs quickly outdated.
  • Lack of Version Control (No Git Diff): Binary image files cannot be compared line-by-line in Pull Requests, making architectural reviews cumbersome and error-prone.

The purpose of this article is to introduce the Diagrams as Code (DaC) methodology using Mermaid.js — transforming diagrams into declarative, plain-text scripts that live right alongside source code, render natively on GitHub/GitLab, and version-control effortlessly.
sections.architecture-principles:
The core principle of Mermaid.js is using a declarative text syntax to construct an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), which is then dynamically compiled into crisp, scalable vector graphics (SVG). Here are the most essential diagram families used in software engineering:

  • 1. Flowchart & Architecture Graph: Visualizes data flows, infrastructure topologies, or component hierarchies. Supports TD (Top-Down), LR (Left-Right) orientations and modular subgraph clusters.
  • 2. Sequence Diagram: Exceptionally powerful for modeling protocol handshakes, inter-service REST/gRPC calls, and lifecycle events. Supports autonumber, actor, participant, branching alt/else blocks, and loop constructs.
  • 3. Git Graph: Programmatically maps branching workflows (GitFlow / Trunk-based development), commit histories, and merge/rebase points.
  • 4. Class & Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD): Defines database schemas, foreign keys, cardinality, and object-oriented class relationships.
flowchart LR
    subgraph SourceCode [Source Code and Markdown Docs]
        MD[README.md / Tech Spec]
        MermaidCode[Mermaid Code Block]
    end

    subgraph CompilerEngine [Mermaid Engine Parser]
        Lexer[Lexer and Parser]
        AST[Diagram Abstract Syntax Tree AST]
    end

    subgraph RenderTarget [Vector Rendering Output]
        SVG[Crisp Scalable SVG]
        InteractiveUI[Fit View and Dark Theme Support]
    end

    MD --> MermaidCode
    MermaidCode --> Lexer
    Lexer --> AST
    AST --> SVG
    SVG --> InteractiveUI
sections.step-by-step-setup:
Step-by-step workflow for integrating Mermaid.js into engineering repositories and doc toolchains:

  • Step 1 - Declare Mermaid fenced code blocks: Use standard ```mermaid fences in any Markdown document. Platforms such as GitHub, GitLab, Notion, and Obsidian provide native out-of-the-box rendering.
  • Step 2 - Model Git branching workflows:
    gitGraph
    commit id: "v1.0.0"
    branch develop
    checkout develop
    commit id: "feat: auth-service"

sections.troubleshooting-pitfalls:
When authoring complex Mermaid diagrams, watch out for these three common pitfalls:

  • 1. Special Characters in Text Labels: If node labels contain nested parentheses () or square brackets [], the parser may confuse them with node boundary syntax. Solution: Avoid nested brackets or use hyphens/slashes to separate label details: NodeA[Node Title - Extra Details].
  • 2. HTML Entity Escaping: When Markdown preprocessors convert < to < or > to >, sanitize and decode HTML entities before passing the string to mermaid.render().
  • 3. Layout Overflow on High-Density Graphs: Avoid placing 50+ services on a single flat canvas. Segment the topology using modular subgraph groups or divide them across bounded domain contexts.
sections.evaluation-scaling:
Evaluation & Future Outlook:

  • Engineering Productivity ROI: Reduces diagram maintenance time by over 80%. Architectural updates are reviewed and tracked directly via standard Git commits and pull requests.
  • Automated Diagram Generation (AST to Diagrams): Pair OpenAPI/Swagger specs or TypeScript AST parsers to auto-generate class diagrams and API flow charts directly from code without manual drawing.
  • Universal Cross-Platform Vector Fidelity: SVG output guarantees crisp rendering on Retina/4K displays and enables custom styling via CSS theme variables.

title: 3-Tier DRY Frontend Architecture: Component Hierarchy & Decoupled Business Service Layer
summary: A comprehensive architectural guide to structuring scalable React/TypeScript applications with a 3-tier UI hierarchy (Primitives -> Specialized -> Composite) and a decoupled Business Service layer.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.context-problem:
As Single Page Applications (SPAs) scale in feature set, a common architectural anti-pattern is the 'God Component'—a state where presentation, UI state, routing, and data hydration/fetching logic are tightly entangled.

In the legacy codebase, components like BlogSection and App.tsx shouldered excessive responsibilities: managing theme/routes, parsing raw HTML headings, filtering articles, and rendering cards directly. This violated the Single Responsibility Principle, introduced WET duplication, and resulted in bloated, fragile unit tests.
sections.system-requirements:
To resolve these structural bottlenecks, the target architecture had to fulfill four fundamental engineering requirements:

  • 1. Strict Separation of Concerns: Distinct boundaries between Common Primitives, Specialized UI Extensions, Composite Component Widgets, Pure Business Services, and Page Views.
  • 2. Systematic DRY Compliance: Eliminate repeated layout, buttons, and modal logic through pure Component Composition.
  • 3. Decoupled Business Service Layer: Month/year archive glob loaders, article hydration, and assembling structured HTML dictionaries must reside in pure TypeScript services independent of React component lifecycles.
  • 4. 100% Type Safety & High Testability: Clear interfaces for every entity, enabling isolated unit testing without cumbersome DOM mocking.
sections.architecture-design:
I established a 3-Tier DRY UI component hierarchy coupled with an independent Business Service Layer as illustrated below:

graph TD
    subgraph PagesLayer [Pages Layer - Screen Views]
        Home[Home Page]
        Blog[Blog Page]
    end

    subgraph ServiceLayer [Business Service Layer - Pure Logic]
        BlogService[BlogService]
        ThemeUtils[Theme and Utils]
    end

    subgraph UILayers [3-Tier DRY Component Hierarchy]
        subgraph CompositeTier [Tier 3: Composite Layer]
            BlogItem[BlogItem]
            ModalArticle[ModalArticle / ModalCaseStudy]
            DrawerMenu[DrawerMenu / FloatingActions]
            BadgesComp[BadgeFilterChip / BadgeSchedule]
        end

        subgraph UITier [Tier 2: Specialized UI Layer]
            Section[Section / SectionHeader]
            InputSearch[InputSearch]
            ButtonFloating[ButtonFloating]
        end

        subgraph CommonTier [Tier 1: Common Primitives]
            Button[Button]
            Card
            Modal[Modal]
            Badge[Badge]
            Input[Input]
        end
    end

    Home --> CompositeTier
    Blog --> CompositeTier
    Blog --> BlogService
    CompositeTier --> UITier
    CompositeTier --> CommonTier
    UITier --> CommonTier

Architectural Responsibilities by Layer:

  • Tier 1 - Common Primitives (src/components/common): Foundational atoms (Button, Card, Badge, Input, Modal) that are purely stateless or contain minimal UI-state, strictly following design tokens and semantic HTML elements.
  • Tier 2 - Specialized UI (src/components/ui): Extended from Tier 1 with specialized styling and behaviors (e.g. InputSearch with built-in search icon and clear trigger, ButtonFloating with glow and ripple effects).
  • Tier 3 - Composite Components (src/components/composite): Composed widgets combining Tier 1 & Tier 2 elements into fully functional business blocks. E.g. BlogItem packaging Card + Badge + TechTagList + read button; ModalArticle packaging Modal + TocSidebar scrollspy.
  • Business Services (src/services): Houses pure business logic (dynamic glob loaders, date parsing, section assemblers), freeing UI components to focus solely on presentation.
  • Pages Layer (src/pages): Encapsulates complete screens (Home.tsx, Blog.tsx), reducing App.tsx into a lean Root Router.
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Architectural Trade-offs & Benefits:

  • Gained Benefits:
    • High Reusability: Global styling or behavior updates for buttons, cards, or modals only happen in a single place within common/.
    • Maintainability & Extensibility: Adding new pages or blog tracks requires zero modifications to existing components.
    • Testability: 100% isolated unit test coverage per layer.
  • Trade-off Costs:
    • Increased File Count: Requires rigorous directory discipline and maintained barrel exports (index.ts).
    • Team Discipline: Strict prohibition of upward imports (a lower tier component must never import from an upper tier).
sections.lessons-best-practices:
Key Practical Takeaways & Best Practices:

  • Favor Composition over Inheritance: Use Compound Component patterns (e.g. Card.Header, Card.Body, Card.Footer) instead of overwhelming prop lists.
  • Consistent Naming Conventions: Adopting prefix-based inheritance names like ModalCaseStudy, BadgeSchedule, ButtonFloatingScrollTop makes component origin and tier instantly obvious.
  • Eliminate Layout Coupling in Reusable Styles: Avoid hardcoding display layout properties (inline flex styles) on base cards so consumer containers retain full layout autonomy (Grid or Flexbox).

title: Optimizing Performance & Integrating Mermaid.js in Modern Web UI: Dark Theme Synchronization, Viewport Fit View & Responsive Ergonomics
summary: The craft of embedding dynamic Mermaid.js in React/TypeScript SPAs: On-demand ESM loading, high-contrast Dark Mode synchronization, interactive Pan/Zoom Fit View, and seamless text-flow integration.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement:
Embedding dynamic architectural and sequence diagrams into technical blogs and documentation portals creates an engaging reading experience. However, integrating mermaid into a React/TypeScript Single Page Application (SPA) presents four significant engineering hurdles:

  • 1. Bundle Size Bloat: Mermaid bundles heavy layout and parsing engines (Dagre, Cytoscape, KaTeX, D3) totaling over 1.4MB. Static top-level imports severely degrade First Contentful Paint (FCP).
  • 2. Dark Mode Contrast Invisibility: In dark theme, default SVG text fills and line strokes blend into dark card backgrounds, rendering diagrams illegible.
  • 3. Mobile Viewport Constraints: Complex microservice topologies or multi-actor sequence diagrams either shrink into unreadable sizes or overflow horizontally.
  • 4. Artificial Box Isolation: Wrapping diagrams in heavy card borders and shadows makes illustrations feel disjointed from the surrounding narrative.
sections.initial-approach:
Common naive integration patterns in React applications:

  • Static import import mermaid from 'mermaid' with synchronous execution on initial mount.
  • Wrapping rendered diagrams in bordered card containers with heavy box shadows.
  • Using default presets (theme: 'default') without synchronizing with custom Design Tokens.

Why this fails in practice: Diagrams cannot dynamically update when toggling themes during reading sessions. Mobile users cannot pan or zoom into high-density flows, and rigid card borders disrupt typography rhythm.
sections.optimization-thinking:
To deliver an uncompromised reader experience, I engineered an end-to-end integration architecture:

  • 1. Dynamic On-Demand ESM Loading: Load the Mermaid bundle only when an article actually contains pre.mermaid code blocks, backed by a resilient fallback mechanism.
  • 2. Theme Synchronization & High-Contrast CSS: Utilize theme: 'base' with complete Ruby/Crimson design variables and scoped CSS rules (> svg) to enforce crisp #f8fafc text labels in Dark Mode.
  • 3. Viewport Fit View Modal: An interactive, compact micro-pill button triggers full-viewport expansion (95vw x 86vh) equipped with 60 FPS GPU-accelerated Pan and Zoom (40% - 350%).
  • 4. Seamless Text-Flow Integration: Eliminate heavy box borders and backgrounds, allowing vector diagrams to breathe naturally between paragraphs.
sections.code-implementation:
Implementation workflow across React components and SCSS:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Reader as Reader (User)
    participant Article as ModalArticle.tsx
    participant ThemeObs as MutationObserver data-theme
    participant MermaidEngine as Mermaid.js Dynamic ESM
    participant Viewer as ModalDiagramViewer.tsx

    Reader->>Article: Opens article containing diagrams
    Article->>MermaidEngine: On-demand import and render SVG with theme base
    MermaidEngine-->>Article: Injects crisp SVG and Fit View micro-pill
    opt User toggles Dark or Light theme
        ThemeObs->>Article: Captures data-theme attribute change
        Article->>MermaidEngine: Instant re-render with updated contrast palette
    end
    opt User clicks diagram or presses Enter
        Reader->>Article: Triggers click or keyboard focus
        Article->>Viewer: Launches Fullscreen Fit View Overlay
        Viewer-->>Reader: Interactive 60 FPS Pan and Zoom experience
    end

Key Engineering Takeaways:

  • CSS Child Selector Scoping (> svg): Prevents diagram container sizing rules from overriding micro-icons inside button pills.
  • Theme Synchronization via MutationObserver: Automatically captures root theme switches to refresh vector colors without page reloads.
sections.complexity-applications:
Performance & Production Impact:

  • GPU Hardware Acceleration: Pan and Zoom operations in the diagram viewer utilize transform: translate3d(...) scale(...) on the browser's GPU compositing layer, maintaining a steady 60 FPS.
  • Bundle Optimization: Dynamic code-splitting eliminates 1.4MB+ of JavaScript on pages without diagrams.
  • Versatile Applications: This pattern sets the benchmark for enterprise documentation systems, API developer portals, and interactive technical blogs.
